title: Model Selection Decision V1
description: The body-free record of which model a request was governed onto. This is the accounting and audit view, not the gateway's decision: the gateway selects the model and the local selector is its proven-equivalent reference. What this document adds is what a usage record needs and the gateway does not carry, namely provider identity on both sides and the quality of the calling application's attribution.

decision.description: 'unavailable' means the record could not be completed, not that the request failed. A request may have been served while the catalogue needed to describe it was absent.

hops.description: Downgrade is single step, so this is 0 or 1. A longer ladder is a documented extension point rather than a shipped behaviour.

modelIdentity.description: Provider identity is stated on both sides so a provider change can never be implicit. It is null only when the catalogue could not supply it, and that case is always accompanied by an unavailable decision.

breachedScopes.description: Budget pressure is measured whether or not a downgrade was configured, because those are separate facts and an audit record needs the second one even when no plan exists.

applicationAttribution.description: Present on every branch, including an unavailable one, because an unavailable decision is still attributed to a caller.

quality.description: 'strong' is a reviewed client-specific registration or application role. 'generic' is a shared developer tool. Null means the catalogue could not resolve the caller, and a null is never presented as a specific coding agent.

exhausted.description: Why budget pressure produced no downgrade. Without the blocking class, a user-facing reason degrades to 'fallback did not happen', which an administrator cannot act on.

unenforcedPolicy.description: A plan that compiled to nothing and a deployment with no plan reach the request path identically, so a configured denial can be asked for and not carried out. Recording it as a denial would describe something that did not happen; omitting it would hide the gap from the auditor who configured it.
